name: The IKEA Effect
statement: We value the things we build ourselves more than they are objectively worth.
meaning: The IKEA effect is the tendency to place a disproportionately high value on products one has partly created or assembled oneself. The labour we put into something raises how much we like it and what we think it is worth, even when the result is mediocre. Named for the flat-pack furniture that arrives needing assembly, it shows that effort alone, not just the quality of the outcome, can make us prize the fruits of our own work.
mechanism: Several forces combine. Effort justification leads us to value what we worked for, and successful assembly signals competence and a sense of control, meeting a basic need to produce effects in our environment. These add to the ordinary endowment effect of owning something. Crucially, the boost requires successful completion: labour that ends in failure, or is stopped short, does not raise valuation and can even lower it. So it is completed effort, not effort in general, that turns labour into love.

examples.text: In the founding studies, people who assembled plain storage boxes bid more for them and liked them more than those who received the same boxes pre-built.
People valued origami they had folded themselves nearly as much as expert-made pieces, while outside observers valued the amateurs' work far less.
The old story that instant cake mixes sold better once they required adding an egg is a popular illustration, though the authors themselves hedge it as contested.

variants.name: The completion condition
variants.text: The boundary that labour raises valuation only when it succeeds; unbuilding one's creation or stopping before finishing erases the effect.

variants.name: Beyond the endowment effect
variants.text: The finding that self-assembly adds value over and above mere ownership, distinguishing the IKEA effect from simply possessing an object.

whyItMatters: It matters for marketing and product design, showing that inviting customers to co-create or assemble can raise what they are willing to pay and how attached they feel. It informs customization strategies and the psychology of ownership and motivation, and it captures a broadly useful truth about human valuation: our own effort, when it succeeds, makes things feel more valuable than a detached appraisal would allow.

working.text: invite customers or users to invest successful effort in a product to raise their valuation and attachment.
design the task so people can finish successfully, since incomplete or failed labour does not produce the effect and can reduce liking.
recognise that your effort inflates your estimate of what you have made, and seek an outside appraisal when it matters.

limits: It is well supported with clearly demonstrated boundary conditions, but the original studies used modest samples and small, inexpensive items, and the authors note that generalisation to expensive goods is untested. The effect requires successful completion; failed or undone labour does not produce it. Its comparison with the endowment effect should be stated carefully, since in the original studies the endowment condition's difference was not statistically significant, so the claim is that the IKEA effect exceeded a here-weak endowment effect.
misreadings: It does not require the result to be well made; the effect holds for often poorly constructed creations, with amateurs valuing their work near expert levels. It is not merely the endowment effect, since self-assembly adds value beyond ownership. It is not just customization, since it appears even for standardized, non-customizable items. And not any effort works: without successful completion, the effect vanishes.
origin: Coined and demonstrated by Michael Norton, Daniel Mochon, and Dan Ariely, circulated as a 2011 working paper and published as 'The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love' in the Journal of Consumer Psychology in 2012.

sources.text: Norton, Mochon & Ariely, "The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love," Journal of Consumer Psychology 22 (2012): 453-460. — the definition, experiments, and completion condition.
IKEA effect, Wikipedia. — the self-made valuation boost, its mechanisms, and its boundary conditions.
